    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    ’Tis the season to embrace all things cozy, and that includes gingerbread. The scent isn’t just wafting from our ovens and favorite coffee shops anymore. It’s showing up in our everyday lives, too, as gingerbread fragrances grow more popular.

    In perfume, gingerbread is a gourmand accord: warm ginger, molasses, and cinnamon, usually rounded out with vanilla or woods. Ginger is a clever ingredient. Perfumers often use it as a top note, where it adds sparkle and energy, and it pairs beautifully with pepper, citrus, rich woods, and amber. That’s why a good gingerbread perfume can feel cozy without turning into a candle.

    Leave it to Squishmallows to create the cutest gingerbread fragrance, complete with a vintage-inspired Cam the Cat bottle. This cozy scent blends ginger, coffee biscuit, and caramel for a sweet, snuggly treat that smells like a warm bakery on a chilly morning.

    Jo Malone’s Ginger Biscuit is back for the holiday season. This warm, spicy scent blends ginger, cinnamon, and roasted hazelnut, giving your fragrance wardrobe a cozy, bakery-fresh addition that’s perfect for chilly days.

    For on-the-go delight, this travel-size spray delivers warm sweetness with a hint of citrus zest. Slip it into your bag for a quick spritz of holiday cheer whenever you need it.

    A scent that’s sure to put you in a festive mood, Baked Gingerbread & Brown Sugar makes holiday spritzing feel extra sweet, cozy, and celebratory.

    Although it’s not entirely inspired by gingerbread, this Dior Spice Blend fragrance feels luxuriously rich, with notes of fresh rum, black pepper, and a ginger accord.

    Freshly made gingerbread dough comes to mind with every whiff of this unisex fragrance. Described as a golden embrace, the scent feels familiar yet unexpected. It’s heartwarming yet sensual, and it lingers on the skin long after the holidays are over.

    General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Thejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    Ransomware Attacks Move Beyond Enterprise Systems to Theaten Employees' Families

    📅 28 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (448 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Thejournal

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Attackers are exploiting enterprises' own artificial intelligence systems and extending pressure beyond internal networks to employees and their families, according to a upcoming Semperis survey of organizations that suffered disruptive ransomware attacks.
    • In a recent announcement, the company highlighted findings from its 2026 Ransomware Risk Report, which examines AI-related attack tactics, personal intimidation, and recovery preparedness.
    • Sources indicate that the sample has an important limit: This year's study included only organizations where at least one ransomware attack caused business disruption.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Attackers are exploiting enterprises' own artificial intelligence systems and extending pressure beyond internal networks to employees and their families, according to a upcoming Semperis survey of organizations that suffered disruptive ransomware attacks.

    In a recent announcement, the company highlighted findings from its 2026 Ransomware Risk Report, which examines AI-related attack tactics, personal intimidation, and recovery preparedness. Censuswide surveyed 1,200 information technology and security professionals across nine countries and eight industry sectors in the first half of 2026.

    Sources indicate that the sample has an important limit: This year's study included only organizations where at least one ransomware attack caused business disruption. The results describe those victims' experiences, rather than the likelihood that an organization will suffer an attack. The report says that sampling approach changed from previous studies.

    Semperis sells identity security, recovery and crisis management products.

    In a recent development, the report notes 84% of respondents experienced attacks that exploited AI in some way. Its breakdown distinguishes AI-based attacks, reported by 40%, from attacks that manipulated victims' own AI agents or systems, reported by 44%. That distinction matters: The broader figure covers both attackers using AI and attackers exploiting AI deployed inside an organization.

    In a recent development, defensive use of AI also produced mixed responses. Nearly half of respondents, 49%, mentioned they successfully used AI for detection or response, while 23% said their AI tools failed to detect or respond successfully. Those are survey responses about victimized organizations, rather than a controlled comparison of security products.

    Chris Inglis, former U.S. national cyber director and a Semperis strategic adviser, described the difficulty of recognizing AI's involvement. "Many attacks are not perceived as being aided and abetted by AI because they're just too slick, too sophisticated," he mentioned in the report.

    Sources indicate that data erasure, destruction, or release remained the most frequently reported threat, at 56%. Blackmail, extortion or public shaming followed at 41%, with system lockouts or operational sabotage at 40%. The report also recorded psychological intimidation at 23% and physical threats at 17%.

    As threat actors adopt more targeted and convincing tactics, education leaders need practical ways to reduce risk without undermining the open, connected environments their institutions depend on.

    Nearly 70% of organizations report a significant gap between artificial intelligence spending and measurable financial returns, according to a recent survey by IDC.

    OpenAI has introduced GPT-6 Astra, its most capable broadly deployed model and the first system the company says has reached the "Critical" cybersecurity capability threshold under its Preparedness Framework.

    Network-provider trust concerns are impacting enterprise AI aims, with AI and data-driven projects the most affected initiatives among respondents reporting disruption, according to a report from telecommunications provider Arelion.
